<description>
DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::TopUpWithDB() expands the descriptor from m_max_cached_index + 1, which is 0 for a freshly imported descriptor regardless of its range_start. Importing a descriptor with "range": [N, M] therefore derives and watches every index in [0, M), so the cost of an import is O(M) rather than O(M - N) and the wallet treats scriptPubKeys below N as its own. Load() only expands [range_start, range_end), so those scriptPubKeys stop being IsMine the next time the wallet is opened, and a transaction picked up for one of them during the import rescan is no longer credited to the wallet.

Since ParseDescriptorRange() only bounds the size of the range and not its start, "range": [2146483648, 2147483647] is accepted and expands 2^31 indexes into m_map_script_pub_keys before the RPC returns.

Start the top up loop at range_start and record the index that was actually cached instead of counting from -1, so that Load() and TopUpWithDB() agree on m_max_cached_index for descriptors with a non-zero range_start. Before this change Load() left m_max_cached_index at range_end - range_start - 1 for such descriptors, which made the first top up after opening the wallet re-expand the stored range.

Importing wpkh(xpub/0/*) with "range": [600000, 600009] into a blank watch-only wallet goes from 19.5s to 0.09s on this machine.
</description>

I built this commit and its parent 4bacf21a13 and, on regtest, imported `wpkh(tpub/0/*)` with `"range": [1000, 1009]` and timestamp 0 into a blank watch-only wallet, after paying the addresses at index 0, 999 and 1000. The addresses for indexes 0, 999, 1000, 1009, 1010, 1999 and 2000 come from bip32-descriptors, a BIP32 and descriptor library I maintain, so the boundary is checked without relying on `deriveaddresses`; Core agreed on all seven and on the checksum.

On the parent, indexes 0 and 999 are mine right after the import, with 6 BTC trusted and three transactions; after `unloadwallet`/`loadwallet` both turn false and the wallet shows 2 BTC and one transaction. With this PR it shows 2 BTC and one transaction before and after the reload, index 1000 being the first owned. A wallet written by the parent and opened by this commit also shows 2 BTC, so existing wallets end up where a reload already puts them today. Importing `[600000, 600009]` with timestamp "now" took 21.0 s on the parent and 0.03 s here, in line with the description. The new functional test fails on the parent at the below-start check and passes here.

Ralph's report takes the timing as the author's own and suggests a cache-end unit test; this adds the timing reproduced, the range boundary checked against a second derivation, and the upgrade path from a wallet the old code wrote.
